abstract: Despite their widely different anatomies, the digestive tracts of all animals must perform a set of core functions that allow the animal to acquire and utilize nutrients from the environment. Whether there are general principles that govern how these functions are spatially organized, however, remains unclear. Here we show that the digestive tract of the tunicate Ciona robusta is organized into pigmented and unpigmented domains specialized for nutrient uptake and metabolism, respectively. We identify the major pigment as halocynthiaxanthin, a diet-derived carotenoid that accumulates in the vacuolated, microvilli-rich epithelium of the pigmented domains, marking the absorptive regions along the gut. We find a similar spatial separation of uptake and metabolism in a distantly related tunicate, Styela clava, despite a markedly different pigmentation pattern, as well as in the mouse small intestine along both the anterior-posterior and crypt-villus axes. These findings suggest that the spatial separation of uptake from metabolism is a conserved principle of chordate gut organization. We propose that the underlying trade-off between these two functions may have served as an organizing force in the evolution of specialized digestive cell types and organs.
